Hi all,

I'm trying to decide between my results using a hazard-rate and half-
normal key functions.  Only a few of them have an AIC that
is "significantly" different from the other.  And I'm wondering how
signifcant that difference is because based on the AIC I'd go with one key
function, but going based on covariance I'd go with the other.  There is a
population difference of almost 3,500 between them.  Which key function
should I go with?

messages.subject: Re: Significance
messages.body_plain:
Mike:

Remember that precision of an estimate is not a model selection tool; it
is part of the result from an estimate.  It's a bit like peeking at the
answers in the back of the book to see if you've gotten the correct
answer.  Besides, you seem to imply from your spreadsheet your are
inclined to having estimates with small CVs (CV by the way is the
abbreviation for 'coefficient of variation,' not 'covariance'); someone
else might prefer to have estimates with large CVs (what statisticians
call being 'conservative').  Therefore, there is no clear rule about how
to apply measures of precision in model selection.

Besides, using measures of precision as a means of choosing between
models is unorthodox, and as such, you'd need to go to some length in
your Methods section to convince your audience that you should be using
a method of model selection that nearly no one else uses.

Hence, the answer that causes least consternation is 'select the model
with the smallest AIC.'  Consult pages 69-70 of the Introduction to
Distance Sampling text by Buckland et al. (2001) for more clarification
about bias and precision.

Mike Calkins wrote:

> >Hi all,
> >
> >I'm trying to decide between my results using a hazard-rate and half-
> >normal key functions.  Only a few of them have an AIC that
> >is "significantly" different from the other.  And I'm wondering how
> >signifcant that difference is because based on the AIC I'd go with one key
> >function, but going based on covariance I'd go with the other.  There is a
> >population difference of almost 3,500 between them.  Which key function
> >should I go with?
> >

> >

messages.subject: Re: Significance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike, List,

A few comments about your question:

> > I'm trying to decide between my results using a hazard-rate and half-

> > normal key functions.  Only a few of them have an AIC that is=20
> > "significantly" different from the other.  And I'm wondering how=20
> > signifcant that difference is because based on the AIC I'd go with one=20

> > key function, but going based on covariance I'd go with the other.
> >

I'm assuming you mean CV (coeficient of variation) rather than=20
covariance, from your attached table.

> > There is a population difference of almost 3,500 between them.  Which=20

> > key function should I go with?

> > =20
> >
It's almost impossible to decide which model to use without looking at=20
the data, knowing what is behind them (i.e. are these line or point=20
transects, did basic assumptions hold, what was the design used, field=20
procedures, etc). Sometimes the best model by AIC is not necessarilly=20
the one you want to use, say if you suspect that the fit of a given=20
model is best due to assumption failure of some sort.

But I believe two points are important, and you should consider them=20
carefully:
1) Did you expect detection to vary by site? Did you compared AIC of an=20
analysis pooling data across sites?
2) From your table, density results seem fairly similar for both models=20
for 8 out of 10 sites, which is good. However, for two sites, namelly=20
R28 and especially NW (with 4 times higher density in the case of HR)=20
there must be something going on. I suspect a very awkward HR model is=20
being fitted in NW, but it's difficult to say without looking at it.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Problems with survey design
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, we are having some problems with DISTANCE that we can't solve, =
so maybe there is something simple that we are doing wrong.

We are providing advice to the federal Wildlife Agency on a survey of =
vicu=F1as and guanacos (2 species of camelids) that will be conducted =
starting in March in 6 different provinces of Argentina, a huge effort =
as you can imagine.
We are always facing the same problem with the road issue because it is =
a western and highly rugged area of the country, sometimes working at =
13000-14000 feet.=20

In spite of that, line transects will be used and we are developing the =
survey design. We will try to find a compromise with some transects =
along part of roads (some of them can't be called roads since they are =
so uggly to traverse) and some other transects offroads, but always on =
4x4 trucks.=20

Based on the previous knowledge of the people from each of the =
provinces, we have drawn on paper maps, polygons of relative densities =
for guanacos and vicu=F1as. Some provinces have three classes: high, low =
and null (no animals), and some other have 4 classes: high, medium, low =
and nul. We will not conduct transects in the areas with no animals =
(they might be a few in some sectrors but in such a low density that it =
is useless for estimation purposes). This means we will concentrate on =
the othr polygons, allocating a higer proportion of effort in the high =
density polygons.=20
We digitized those paper maps in a GIS using ArcView and generated the =
shapes for those polygons.

We were planning to use the Systematic Segmented Trackline Sampling =
design pointing at a numerous, but short number of transects to try to =
lower the variance of the encounter rate.
In our case we have 15 different polygons, which we call "strata" =
although several of those belong to the HIGH strata and some to the LOW =
strata, but they are separate pieces of land in a matrix of NO animals =
(NULL sector), which is most of the province.=20

Once we generated coverage grids and tried to run surveys we get several =
errors that stop the process.=20

Following we are copying some of the details of our data and efforts to =
run teh coverage and the designs. Any clues or ideas that anyone could =
provide us to figure out what is wrong will be deeply appreciated and =
extremely helpful.

Thanks !!!

Mart=EDn Funes and Nito Gonzalez

Wildlife Conservation Society
Jun=EDn de los Andes
PATAGONIA, ARGENTINA

messages.subject: For Archives
messages.body_plain:
Len asked me to send the solution to the questions I posted on this list.  I
received a reply directly, and then spent a little more time playing with the
structure of my data.  In the end, I got Program Distance to work by importing
the data set up as a column with the treatment type and a column with the
distance.  Originally, I had used a third column with my point id numbers,
which resulted in an error when I tried to run an analysis.  The error message
read something like "The column with Area does not exist."  That's why I was
asking how to input the area of the points. Structuring my data more simply
cleared the problem up.  Below is the reply I received, which addresses some
specific questions that I had posed in my message.

Claire Crow

> > My point counts stations were not set up along transects, and were
> > visited in a  different order each time

Visit order is inconsequential.

> > program Distance is set up for points taken along  transects.

It handles point data just fine.  Remember that a point is just a
transect of length = 0.

> > Will the difference in sample size in any way affect the program's density
> > estimates?

No.  Just more distances for estimating the detection fucntion.

> > And how do I input the area of the points into the program?

You don't.  As part of estimating density it estimates effective area
surveyed.

messages.subject: another question about factors (summary of answers)
messages.subject_clean: another question about factors (summary of answers)
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone who replied to my factors questions. Here is my =
original question and below is a summary of the answers:=20
*************
Hi again,

Yesterday I asked about why Distance would generate more than one
category for each level of a factor (vegetation type). It turns out that
the factors have to be sorted and grouped, otherwise the program
recognizes each new group as a new level. Thanks to the people who
replied to my inquiry. So this brings me to another question. What if I
want to use two factors as a covariate in an analysis?  Let's say for
example that I have 6 vegetation types and 3 forest stages
(early-successional, mid-successional, and old-growth). These factors
are not fully nested because each vegetation type may have
representation in several or all successional stages, and vice versa. So
when I sort the data by vegetation type the forest stages will be
unsorted and vice-versa. Does this mean that I cannot have two factors
as covariates in an analysis?
=20

Thanks for your input,

=20

Christine
***********************

Summary of answers:

1) Any factor should be ordered before been imported into Distance. If =
they are not ordered, the program will recognize every new "encounter" =
with the same level as a new category.

2) This means that if you have more than one column with categories, you =
need to combine them into one. For example, if you wanted to have =
vegetation type and forest age you would create a column that has =
vegetation type1-forest age1, vegetation type1-forest age2, etc.

Here is a particularly useful answer from Jeff Laake:

Christine-

Not sure where you are going with this.  Are your factors really strata =
for which you want to estimate density?  That is different than using a =
factor variable in the model for detection probability.  Distance is not =
particularly sophisticated with it's handling of designs because its =
original intent was simply to estimate abundance/density rather than as =
a tool to investigate relationships between density and ecological =
factors or for experimental design.  Clearly, this has become a drawback =
because it is a natural evolution of thought and analysis.  =
Unfortunately, the software is lagging and it is something we are trying =
to correct.

If your goal is to estimate density for a set of vegetation x forest =
stages and these can be represented as discrete regions, then I would =
suggest that you create a variable you could call strata which would =
have has its value the possible pairings of vegetation and forest =
stages.  If you then sorted by strata and then lines/points within =
strata, it should work fine.  You can keep the forest stage and =
vegetation as factor variables for modelling detection probability.  If =
your forest stage-vegetation data don't represent specific regions that =
you sampled but each line/point is in a forest/vegetation type you are =
still okay but you'll only want to compare densities and NOT estimate =
abundance for each strata.  If you have line transect data and each =
observation has a forest/veg type you are currently out of luck but in =
the upcoming D6 it will contain a spatial modelling component.  Len/Eric =
may have more to add here when they get time.

--jeff

Hope this helps other people,

Christine

--
